                             CONSOLIDATED CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
 1
 2          Plaintiffs Amorey Walker, Bryce Foster-Quarles and Jamal Qureshi (“Plaintiffs”), bring

 3   this Class Action Complaint individually, and on behalf of all others similarly situated, against

 4   Defendant Sony Interactive Entertainment LLC, (“Defendant”, “Sony”). Plaintiffs allege the

 6
     allegations that specifically pertain to Plaintiffs, which are alleged upon personal knowledge.
 7
                        I.     INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY OF THE CASE
 8
          1.        Plaintiffs bring this class action complaint against Sony for its retention of a
 9
10   substantial windfall generated by unlawful tariffs imposed by the federal government under the

11   International Emergency Economic Powers Act (“IEEPA”), 50 U.S.C. § 1701, et seq.
12        2.        Beginning in February 2025, the Trump administration imposed sweeping tariffs
13
     on imports from numerous countries under purported authority of the IEEPA. The tariffs
14
     dramatically increased the cost of imported consumer goods sold in the United States.
15
          3.        Major U.S. importers, including Sony, responded by increasing prices on consumer
16
17   goods to offset the cost of these tariffs. As a result, consumers in the U.S. paid higher retail prices

18   for goods reflecting the economic burden of these tariffs.

19        4.        Plaintiffs are such consumers. Plaintiffs purchased a Sony PlayStation Console with
20   a price that included a pass-through of the IEEPA tariffs. Plaintiff Amorey purchased a PlayStation
21
     5 Digital Edition on December 1, 2025, Plaintiff Bryce Foster-Quarles purchased a PlayStation 5
22
     Digital Edition on February 20, 2026, and Plaintiff Qureshi purchased a PlayStation Console on
23
     December 16, 2025. Upon information and belief, the price Plaintiffs paid for the PlayStations
24
25   was higher due to Defendant passing on the cost of IEEPA tariffs.

26
27
28
                             CONSOLIDATED CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT                                2
             Case 3:26-cv-04121-CRB           Document 28        Filed 07/15/26      Page 3 of 19




          5.        On February 20, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court held that President Trump’s IEEPA-
 1
 2   based tariffs are unlawful. Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, 607 U.S.       (2026) (slip op. at 20).

 3        6.        Resulting from that decision, importers who paid those IEEPA-based tariffs –

 4   including Sony – became entitled to refunds of the duties they previously paid to U.S. Customs
 5   and Border Protection (“CBP”). To facilitate the refunds to thousands of U.S. importers – including
 6
     Sony – the CBP created a tariff refund website to manage IEEPA duty refunds following the
 7
     Supreme Court’s February 20, 2026, Learning Resources, Inc. decision.
 8
          7.        The economic reality of the tariff regime, however, is that importers like Sony did
 9
10   not ultimately bear all the costs of the tariffs. Sony, for instance, passed the elevated costs on to

11   U.S. consumers in the form of higher retail prices on one popular product, the Sony PlayStation,
12   beginning on August 21, 2025.
13
          8.        Sony therefore collected the tariff costs from consumers through elevated pricing,
14
     while seeking refunds of the same tariff payments from the federal government.
15
          9.        Unless restrained by this Court, Sony stands to recover the same tariff payments
16
17   twice – once from consumers through higher prices and again from the federal government through

18   tariff refunds, including interest paid by the government on those refunds.

19       10.        This class action lawsuit seeks to prevent such an unjust result.
20       11.        Unlike companies such as FedEx and UPS who have explicitly stated they will pass
21
     tariff refunds back to their customers, Sony has made no such commitment.
22
         12.        Plaintiffs bring this class action on behalf of thousands, if not millions, of U.S.
23
     consumers who purchased Sony’s PlayStation Consoles during the tariff period and who paid
24
25   inflated prices reflecting Sony’s pass-through of unlawful tariffs.

26
27
28
                            CONSOLIDATED CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT                                3
            Case 3:26-cv-04121-CRB           Document 28       Filed 07/15/26     Page 4 of 19




         13.        Plaintiffs seek restitution of these tariff overcharges, together with appropriate
 1
 2   declaratory, injunctive, and monetary relief.

 3                            II.   PARTIES, JURISDICTION & VENUE

 4       14.        Plaintiff Amorey Walker is a resident citizen of Brooklyn, New York. On
 5   December 1, 2025, Plaintiff Walker purchased a PlayStation Console imported from countries
 6
     subject to tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (“IEEPA”).
 7
     Upon information and belief, the purchase price for the goods that Plaintiff Walker purchased from
 8
     Sony was increased to account for the tariffs imposed on those products. Plaintiff Walker would
 9
10   not have paid the increased price if Defendant had not passed the cost of the IEEPA tariffs on to

11   consumers.
12       15.        Plaintiff Bryce Foster-Quarles is a resident citizen of Burnsville, Minnesota. On
13
     February 19, 2026, Plaintiff Foster-Quarles purchased a PlayStation Console imported from
14
     countries subject to tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act
15
     (“IEEPA”). Upon information and belief, the purchase price for the goods that Plaintiff Foster-
16
17   Quarles purchased from Sony was increased to account for the tariffs imposed on those products.

18   Plaintiff Foster-Quarles would not have paid the increased price if Defendant had not passed the

19   cost of the IEEPA tariffs on to consumers.
20       16.        Plaintiff Jamal Qureshi is a resident citizen of Harris County, Texas. On December
21
     16, 2025, Plaintiff Qureshi purchased a Sony PlayStation Console imported from countries subject
22
     to tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (“IEEPA”). The
23
     purchase price for the goods that Plaintiff Qureshi purchased from Sony was increased to account
24
25   for the tariffs imposed on those products. Plaintiff Qureshi would not have paid the increased

26   price if Defendant had not passed the cost of the IEEPA tariffs on to consumers.

27
28

             Case 3:26-cv-04121-CRB            Document 28           Filed 07/15/26      Page 5 of 19




         17.          Defendant Sony Interactive Entertainment LLC is a California limited liability
 1
 2   company with its headquarters and principal place of business at 2207 Bridgepointe Parkway, San

 3   Mateo, California. It is a wholly owned subsidiary of the Japanese consumer electronics and media

 4   conglomerate Sony Corporation and is the owner of the PlayStation digital entertainment brand.
 5       18.          Defendant Sony Interactive Entertainment LLC has four (4) members, who are all
 6
     residents of San Mateo, California. Defendant may be served with process by serving its registered
 7

 9

14

15
     located within this District, Defendant regularly conducts business in this District, and the events,

21
                                    III.   FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS
22
         22.          Sony Interactive Entertainment LLC’s parent company, Sony Group Corporation,
23
     is a global Japanese conglomerate known for its leading roles in electronics, gaming, music, and
24
25   entertainment.

26
27
28
                             CONSOLIDATED CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT                                5
             Case 3:26-cv-04121-CRB              Document 28        Filed 07/15/26       Page 6 of 19




         23.            Headquartered in San Mateo, California, Sony Interactive Entertainment LLC
 1
 2   (“Sony” or “Defendant”) is the global business behind the well-known PlayStation brand,

 3   responsible for the development, production, and sales of both hardware and software. Sony’s most

 4   recent model, the PlayStation 5, has become the best-selling video game console of all time. The
 5   PlayStation 5 console launched on November 12, 2020, and by March 31, 2021, had sold 7.8
 6
     million units.1 Going forward, the PlayStation 5’s popularity has remained strong, selling millions
 7
     of units a year.
 8
         24.            Sony currently produces the PlayStation 5, PlayStation 5 Pro, PlayStation 5 Slim,
 9
10   and PlayStation 5 Slim Digital Edition (the “PlayStation Consoles”).

11       25.            The PlayStation Consoles are manufactured primarily in Japan, China, and
12   Thailand, and then imported into the United States.
13
         26.            Sony is the importer of record of most, if not all, PlayStation Consoles brought into
14
     the U.S. for sale. Thus, imported goods account for nearly all of Sony’s retail sales of PlayStation
15
     Consoles in the U.S.
16
17       27.            Because Sony imported the PlayStation Consoles sold in the U.S. during the Class

18   period, the IEEPA tariffs directly increased the cost of the Consoles sold to U.S. consumers.

19           A. The U.S. IEEPA tariffs imposed on Sony; Sony’s corresponding price hikes of
                their PlayStation Consoles; and, the unconscionable windfall to Sony at the
20              expense of Plaintiff and members of the Class
21
         28.            Beginning in February 2025, President Trump issued a series of executive orders
22
     to impose tariffs on goods imported from most foreign countries, including Canada, Mexico,
23
     China, and other U.S. trading partners. Each executive order was premised on IEEPA authorization
24
25
26   1See Sam Byford, Sony has sold 7.8 million PS5 consoles, The Verge (Apr. 28, 2021),

27   https://www.theverge.com/2021/4/28/22407195/sony-ps5-sales-numbers-q4-2020-earnings.

28
                               CONSOLIDATED CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT                                6
             Case 3:26-cv-04121-CRB           Document 28        Filed 07/15/26      Page 7 of 19




     of the tariffs. President Trump claimed that these tariffs were justified under IEEPA because of a
 1
 2   purported national emergency.

 3       29.        Under the authority of IEEPA, President Trump imposed tariffs of 25% on most

 4   imports from Canada and Mexico, tariffs as high as 145% from China, and a baseline 10% tariff
 5   on nearly all imports to the United States.
 6
         30.        Throughout the relevant period, Sony paid IEEPA tariffs to the CBP. The IEEPA
 7
     tariffs had a substantial impact on the cost of Sony PlayStation Consoles, which are imported from
 8
     tariffed countries, including a majority from China.
 9
10       31.        Sony, for instance, revealed in its earnings report for July to September 2025, that

11   the tariffs impacted Sony’s PlayStation Console production in China, and required Sony to pay
12   nearly $194 million in import-related fees during the July-September 2025 quarter.
13
         32.        Economists and government agencies widely recognize that tariffs are largely borne
14
     by domestic consumers rather than foreign exporters or the importing firms that formally remit the
15
     duties. Economic studies examining recent U.S. tariff regimes consistently find that the cost of
16
17   tariffs is passed through into higher prices paid by U.S. purchasers of imported goods. 2

18       33.        When tariffs increase the cost of imported goods, retailers and other downstream

19   sellers typically raise prices to offset those additional costs. Surveys of U.S. businesses conducted
20   by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York during the recent tariff period found that a large
21
     majority of firms facing tariff-related cost increases passed at least some portion of those costs
22
23
24
25   2 See Julian Hinz et al., America’s Own Goal: Who Pays the Tariffs? Kiel Inst. for the World Econ.

26   Policy Brief (Jan. 19, 2026); see also Mary Amiti, Stephen J. Redding & David Weinstein, The
     Impact of the 2018–2019 Tariffs on Prices and Welfare, 135 J. Econ. Persp. 187 (2020).
27
28
                            CONSOLIDATED CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT                                7
             Case 3:26-cv-04121-CRB            Document 28        Filed 07/15/26      Page 8 of 19




     through to their customers in the form of higher prices.3 Companies consider tariffs to be costs that
 1
 2   are to be incorporated into the pricing structure.

 3       34.         Sony was no exception. Like other companies that faced the massive IEEPA tariffs,

 4   Sony raised its PlayStation Consoles’ prices on August 21, 2025, and then again on April 2, 2026.
 5       35.         Citing inflation and global economic pressures, Sony passed the elevated tariff
 6
     costs on to U.S. consumers in the form of higher retail prices. To offset its substantial tariff bill,
 7
     on August 21, 2025, Sony raised prices for all versions of the PlayStation Consoles to be sold in
 8
     the U.S. by $50. Then, on March 27, 2026, Sony announced it will raise prices once again on its
 9
10   range of PlayStation Consoles for a second time in less than a year. In the U.S., effective April 2,

11   2026, the Sony PlayStation 5 “disc edition” jumped from $549.99 to $649.99, a $100 increase (in
12   addition to the $50 increase that Sony had already implemented on August 21, 2025, on all
13
     PlayStation Consoles). The PlayStation digital edition increased by $100, to $599.99. The U.S.
14
     sales price of the PlayStation 5 Pro, Sony’s most powerful version of the console, increased by
15
     $150, to $899.99.
16
17       36.         On February 20, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court held that the IEEPA tariff regime

18   was unlawful because the IEEPA does not authorize the President to impose such tariffs; the Court

19   thus invalidated all IEEPA-based tariffs. Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, 607 U.S.          (2026)
20   (slip op. at 20).
21
         37.         President Trump subsequently issued an Executive Order terminating the IEEPA
22
     Tariffs, and on February 22, 2026, the CBP issued CSMS #67834313, announcing that it will halt
23
24
25
     3
26    See Jaison R. Abel, Richard Deitz & Jason Bram, Are Businesses Absorbing the Tariffs or Passing
     Them On to Their Customers? Fed. Rsrv. Bank of N.Y., Liberty Street Econ. (June 4, 2025),
27   available at https://libertystreeteconomics.newyorkfed.org.

                            CONSOLIDATED CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT                                 8

     collection of all tariffs imposed pursuant to IEEPA. The termination of IEEPA tariffs took effect
 1
 2   at 12:00 a.m. EST on February 24, 2026.

 3       38.        Consequently, importers who had paid these IEEPA-based tariffs – including Sony

 4   – became entitled to refunds of the duties they had previously paid to the CBP. According to Mr.
 5   Brandon Lord, the Executive Director of CBP’s Trade Programs Directorate, as of March 4, 2026,
 6
     the total amount of IEEPA duties and estimated duty deposits collected pursuant to IEEPA was
 7
     approximately $166 billion. Atmus Filtration, Inc. v. United States, No. 26-01259, Order at 1 (Ct.
 8
     Int’l Trade Mar. 4, 2026), ECF No. 31 at 6.
 9
10       39.        To facilitate refunds of the $166 billion in collected tariffs, the CBP created a tariff

11   refund website – the “Consolidated Administration and Processing of Entries (CAPE) portal”,
12   which went live on Monday, April 20, 2026, at 8 a.m. EST. The CBP expects refunds to be issued
13
     within 60 to 90 days after it accepts a refund application.
14
         40.        Given the substantial amount of IEEPA tariffs Sony paid to the CBP because of
15
     importing the Sony PlayStation Consoles, it is now, understandably, in the process of seeking this
16
17   vast sum of money from the CBP.

18       41.        This presents an obvious problem. Although Sony will recover tariff refunds on the

19   tariffed PlayStation Consoles it sold in the U.S. during the Class period, Sony’s U.S. based
20   customers bore the economic brunt of these tariffs by paying higher prices set by Sony on August
21
     21, 2025, and then on April 2, 2026. Sony obtaining a double recovery windfall is therefore
22
     imminent. Sony is poised to be paid twice for the same unlawful tariff burden: once by its
23
     customers (through elevated prices) and once by the U.S. government (through tariff refunds).
